name: Bolyu
catalog_citation: Edmondson, Jerold A. & Kenneth J. Gregerson. 1996. Bolyu tone in Vietic perspective. Mon-Khmer Studies 26: 117-133.
catalog_locator: p. 118 (§1 Introduction, 2nd paragraph; pdf p. 2), p. 120 (§2 Bolyu Tones, opening; pdf p. 4 — not p. 119/pdf p. 3 as the first reader wrote: the scanned page mark…
catalog_quote: Linguistically, Bolyu fits perfectly into the local linguistic landscape, in the sense that it demonstrates a rich inventory of tone contrasts with mostly monosyllabic roots, only /-p -t -k/ syllable codas, a consonant inventory resembling Zhuang (except for uvular stops and velarized initials), and vowel length contrasts in closed syllables (See Appendix 2:Notes on phonological segments). It doesn’t possess many of the distinctive Mon-Khmer phonological traits such as sesqui-syllabic word structure, a rich system of syllable codas, and voice quality (register) contrasts (see below, however, that the related Bugan language has a tense vs lax opposition). [p. 118] ... Bolyu has six tones, which in various publications have appeared with the following representations: the numbering system by Benedict (1-6), pitch level values (55, 33, etc) by Liang and Ni, and the IPA/Chao tone symbols ..…
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.citation: Edmondson, Jerold A. & Kenneth J. Gregerson. 1996. Bolyu tone in Vietic perspective. Mon-Khmer Studies 26: 117-133.
new_statements.locator: p. 118 (§1 Introduction) and p. 133 (Appendix 2: Notes on phonological segments)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (17-page scan, no text layer; the PDF's metadata confirms) and its scanned (1067 lines). Both quoted passages are there verbatim: the p.118 passage (pdf page 2, §1 Introduction, second paragraph) "Linguistically, Bolyu fits perfectly into the local linguistic landscape.. It doesn't possess many of the distinctive Mon-Khmer phonological traits such as sesqui-syllabic word structure, a rich system of syllable codas, and voice quality (register) contrasts" (print hyphenates "sesqui-/syllabic" at a line break); and the p.133 passage (pdf page 17, Appendix 2: Notes on phonological segments, vowel paragraph) "In many disyllabic words the first vowel shows reduction to [ə]." I rendered both…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-stress rule is stated by any opened source. Bolyu is described as a monosyllabic tone language with six contour tones (55, 33, 11, 53, 31, 13; nine historical categories) and no sesquisyllabic structure; the only prominence-related observation is that in many disyllabic (compound/prefixed) words the first vowel reduces to schwa, i.e. non-final elements are weak. Benedict 1990 (pp. 9, 16) speculates diachronically about 'weak or zero stress' / 'reduced stress' on the prefix ka1- but gives no synchronic rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Edmondson & Gregerson note vowel-length judgements are uncertain and that long-vowel items are usually Han loans.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level remarks on monosyllabic roots and disyllabic compounds/prefixed words in citation forms from a 1990 wordlist (Changmo village, Longlin); no phrase-level prosody discussed. The primary Chinese reference grammar (Li Xulian 1999) was not accessible and may contain a 重音 statement.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe Bolyu of Longlin County, Guangxi: Edmondson (1995, 1996) data from Changmo village (April 1990); Li Xulian 1999 / Hsiu 2016 describe the Muzitun 亩子屯 (Xinhe, Changfa Township) variety; Benedict 1990 and Sidwell 1995 are secondary on Liang 1984 and Edmondson 1995. Glottolog ref 435604 'Ouyang & Zheng 1963, Laiyu gaikuang' is very likely 黎语概况 (Hlai, Hainan; hlai1239 group) mis-assigned to Bolyu, since those authors are Hlai specialists; treat as not a Bolyu source. Bolyu is closely related to Bugan (buga1247/buga1251), which unlike Bolyu has tense/lax register and an atonal prefix prosody (Li Jinfang per Edmondson & Gregerson 1996:119).

new_statements.relation_note: This is the same work that supplies the catalog's existing_statement (reading 'tone language, no stress statement', pp. 118 and 133); a full read of all 17 pages confirms that statement: the paper is about tone and says nothing about word stress. The catalog record for Bolyu has an empty rule, so there is nothing to contradict. download of the listed open_url failed twice (purl.org -> sealang.net: connection refused; the Internet Archive: connection refused, network down by automated download), so the copy already held by the project (Internet Archive copy downloaded earlier in this reading) was read instead.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-stress rule is stated anywhere in the paper. Bolyu is described as a six-tone language (55, 33, 11/21, 53, 31, 13) with mostly monosyllabic roots and no sesquisyllabic word structure; tone, not stress, is the word-level prosody described. The only prominence-adjacent remark is that in many disyllabic words the first vowel reduces to [ə] (p. 133), which implies a weak initial syllable in disyllables but is not framed as stress. The words 'pretonic syllable' / 'tonic syllable' on p. 127 describe historical Vietic forms (Pk sanam, S-Rc capo:), not Bolyu.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. Disyllabic words exist (first vowel reduced to [ə]); Han loanwords carry the few purported vowel-length differences (p. 133).
new_statements.identity_note: Edmondson & Gregerson 1996 describe the Bolyu of Changmo village, Longlin Various Nationalities Autonomous County, western Guangxi (data from Mr. Lu, April 1990); they note the autonym is [pəljuʌ] elsewhere per Liang Min 1984 / Ni Dabai 1990, and treat the related Bugan of Yunnan (Li Jinfang 1995) as a separate language. Correct languoid for boly1239.

sources.citation: Benedict, Paul K. 1990. How to tell Lai: an exercise in classification. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 13(2): 1-26.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Comparative/classificatory paper based on Liang 1984. p.1: typology 'thoroughly Zhuang-Dong (Kam-Tai): monosyllabic morphemes.. six tones (only five before stop finals)'. Only stress mentions are diachronic speculation about the prefix ka1-: p.9 'Perhaps initial *k- was retained here because of the weak or zero stress of this prefix.. in this weakly (zero) stressed element'; p.16 '*k- > k-.. in prefixed ka1-, apparently as the result of reduced stress.' No synchronic word-stress rule. Scan, all 26 pp. scanned.

sources.note: §3.1 Bolyu (pp. 7-9, drawing on Li Xulian 1999, Muzitun dialect): 31 consonants, many palatalized/labialized clusters, 10 vowels with length contrast, '9 tone categories and unique 6 contour tones, namely /11/, /33/, /55/, /31/, /13/, and /53/'; 'monosyllabic syllable structure' shared with Northern Tai.
